name: Otago Farmers Market
description:
One of the country's best-known farmers markets, running every Saturday morning since March 2003 in the northern car park of the grand Dunedin Railway Station. It's a food-only market, with stallholders from around Otago selling bread, cheese, meat, fruit and vegetables, plus hot food and good coffee to eat as you wander.

It's busy and bustling from 8am to 12.30pm, and it makes an easy start to a Saturday before a walk around the station and the city.
Local tip: Try a cheese roll, the southern classic of cheese rolled up in white bread and toasted, which several stalls sell.
hoursNote: Saturdays only, 8am to 12.30pm; northern car park at the Railway Station

name: Beam Me Up Bagels
description:
A small, friendly bagel café with sci-fi names on everything, from the Men in Black to the Red Dwarf. The bagels are soft and chewy, the fillings are generous, and one is enough to keep you going until dinner. The coffee is good too.

This is the city shop on Great King Street North, and the original is in North East Valley near Baldwin Street. Both get busy at lunchtime.
Local tip: Stop at the North East Valley shop on North Road before or after you walk up Baldwin Street, since it's just around the corner.
hoursNote: Daily 8.30am to 2.30pm (both shops)

name: Hungry Hobos
description:
A toasted sandwich shop on George Street, with a long menu of crispy, cheese-heavy toasties in half and full sizes, plus soup. Most half sizes are under $10, and the full sizes are big enough to take half home.

The staff are consistently friendly, and there are comics to read while you wait. It's one of the best cheap lunches in the city.
Local tip: Order the mac and cheese with bacon toastie, and add a cheese roll if you haven't tried one yet.
hoursNote: Opening hours not listed online; check before going, lunch is the safe bet

name: Bacon Buttie Station
description:
A no-frills breakfast and lunch spot on Ward Street, near the Railway Station, doing bacon sandwiches, burgers and cheap all-day breakfasts. It's busy with locals, and regulars rate it as some of the best-value food in the city.

It's simple food done properly rather than a sit-down brunch café, open from 7.30am on weekdays and 9am at weekends until 3pm.
Local tip: The bacon and mushroom burger is the one to get, and it's handy before or after the Saturday farmers market.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 7.30am to 3pm; Sat and Sun 9am to 3pm

name: Vogel St Kitchen
description:
A big, warm café in a restored warehouse in the Warehouse Precinct, with seating downstairs, upstairs and outside. Brunch runs through the morning, and wood-fired pizza and burgers start after 11am. The cabinet of cakes and savouries is good for takeaway too.

It's right in the middle of the street art area, so it's an easy base for a mural walk.
Local tip: Come after 11am if you want the wood-fired pizza, and expect a wait for a table at weekend brunch.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 7.30am to 2.30pm; Sat and Sun 8.30am to 3pm; pizza from 11am

name: Starfish Cafe & Bar
description:
A busy café a block back from St Clair beach, open early every day. It does a solid brunch menu, a full cabinet and good coffee, and it's a go-to after a swim or a surf.

It gets crowded and service can be stretched at peak times, but the food is consistently well rated, and the upstairs seating gets a lot of sun.
Local tip: It opens at 6.30am, so it's ideal for coffee before a dawn walk along the beach or a surf.
hoursNote: Daily 6.30am to 3pm

name: Ric's Galley Fish & Chips, Portobello
description:
A takeaway fish and chip shop in Portobello, about halfway out along the Otago Peninsula, known locally for fresh fish at good prices. People drive out from town for it, and the burgers get praise too.

It's takeaway only and can have a queue when it's busy.
Local tip: Pick up dinner here on the way back from the Royal Albatross Centre, and eat it on the harbour edge in Portobello.
hoursNote: Opening hours not listed online; call ahead, especially in winter

name: Emerson's Brewery
description:
The taproom and restaurant of one of New Zealand's best-known craft breweries, in a big, modern industrial space at 70 Anzac Avenue. Tasting flights let you try several beers, and the food menu runs from fries and fried mushrooms to burgers and mains.

It's lively in the evenings, and there's a shop for merchandise and takeaway beer. Some reviewers find the mains small for the price, so the snacks and flights are the better value.
Local tip: Book a guided tasting if you want the story behind the beers, and note it's closed on Mondays.
hoursNote: Closed Mon; Tue to Sun 11am to 10pm

name: Larnach Castle
description:
New Zealand's only castle, built in 1871 on the ridge of the Otago Peninsula and derelict until the Barker family bought it in 1967 and began restoring it. You can wander the furnished rooms, climb the tower for views over the harbour and peninsula, and explore the gardens, which are rated a Garden of International Significance.

Castle and gardens entry is $50 for adults, $17 for children aged 5 to 14 and $117 for a family, and gardens only is $25 for adults. The Ballroom Café does lunches and high tea, and the drive out along Highcliff Road has big views of its own.
Local tip: Go up to the tower first on a clear day, before the cloud rolls in, then do the gardens and the café.
hoursNote: Listed daily 9am to 5pm; some rooms may be closed for restoration

name: Tūhura Otago Museum
description:
A big museum next to the university, with galleries covering Māori culture, Pacific voyaging, natural history and world cultures, including a huge moa display, a Haast's eagle skeleton, a plesiosaur fossil and an Egyptian mummy. Entry is free for New Zealand residents, and international visitors pay for a gallery pass, about $20 for adults.

The hands-on science centre (from $13) and the planetarium (from $9) cost extra, or from $15 for both. The Tropical Forest butterfly house is closed for maintenance until early December 2026. There's a café and gift shop, and it's open daily from 10am to 5pm.
Local tip: Families find two hours goes very quickly, so allow half a day if you have children, and check the Tropical Forest has reopened before you promise it to them.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm; general entry free, butterfly house, planetarium and science centre extra

name: Toitū Otago Settlers Museum
description:
A free museum telling the story of Otago, from Kāi Tahu and the first Māori settlement to the Scottish settlers, the gold rush and modern Dunedin. It's large and well laid out, with more than a dozen galleries, old vehicles and a play area for kids.

Most visitors are surprised by how much there is, and three hours still isn't enough to see all of it. It's open daily from 10am to 5pm, and donations are welcome.
Local tip: Pair it with the Chinese Garden next door, and the Railway Station and farmers market are a two minute walk away.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm; free entry, donations welcome

name: Dunedin Botanic Garden
description:
New Zealand's first botanic garden, founded in 1863 and free to visit, spread over 28 hectares with more than 6,800 plant species. The flat lower garden has the Edwardian Winter Garden glasshouse, a Japanese garden, formal rose and camellia gardens, a duck pond and a playground, while the hilly upper garden has a huge rhododendron forest, daffodils in spring and an aviary with native and exotic parrots, one of which talks.

The lower garden is flat and wheelchair friendly, but the upper paths are steep. Allow a couple of hours or more.
Local tip: Park at the upper (east) entrance if you mainly want the aviary, and bring a picnic for the lawns.
hoursNote: Open daily; visitor centre from 10am; lower garden flat, upper garden hilly

name: Lan Yuan, Dunedin Chinese Garden
description:
A traditional Chinese scholar's garden built with Shanghai, Dunedin's sister city, to honour the Chinese gold miners who came to Otago in the 1860s. It has ponds, bridges, rockeries and pavilions, plus a tea house where you can sit over a pot of Chinese tea.

Adults are $13.50, students and beneficiaries $10, and children under 13 are free with an adult. It's open daily from 10am to 5pm, there's a free car park, and it's small and calm, taking under an hour.
Local tip: Stop in the tea house, and read the story of how the garden was made in Shanghai and shipped over.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm; closed 25 Dec; free parking on site

name: Baldwin Street
description:
A short residential street in North East Valley, listed by Guinness as the steepest street in the world. Walking up it is a proper workout, and there's a view over the valley and a water tap at the top.

It's a quick, free stop that takes about 20 minutes up and down. People live here, so keep the noise down and don't block driveways.
Local tip: Walk it rather than drive it, park on North Road at the bottom, and reward yourself with a bagel at Beam Me Up around the corner.
hoursNote: Open any time; residential street, be considerate; steep

name: Dunedin Railway Station
description:
Dunedin's best-known building, an ornate Flemish Renaissance style station from the early 1900s, with a mosaic floor and stained glass inside and gardens out front. It's free to walk in, and it's one of the most photographed buildings in New Zealand.

It's still the base for the Taieri Gorge excursion trains, and it hosts the Saturday farmers market in its northern car park. The stained glass looks best in low afternoon light.
Local tip: Come on a Saturday morning and combine it with the farmers market next door.
hoursNote: Building open to walk through during the day; farmers market Saturdays

name: Taieri Gorge Railway
description:
Dunedin's signature train trip, leaving from the historic Dunedin Railway Station at 9.30am and heading inland through the deep, rocky Taieri Gorge, over viaducts and through tunnels, to Pukerangi on the edge of Central Otago. The return trip takes about 5 hours, getting back around 2.15pm, with commentary along the way.

Adults are $169 return and children $59, and infants travel free. Depending on the day and the weather, the train may stop at Hindon or Deep Stream so you can get out, and food and drinks are sold on board. One-way tickets to Pukerangi connect with cycle hire on the Otago Central Rail Trail.
Local tip: Check-in closes at 9.15am, so arrive early to look around the station building before you board, and bring a warm layer for the viewing platform.
hoursNote: Thu to Mon, departs 9.30am from Dunedin Railway Station; about 5 hours return; adult $169, child $59

name: Dunedin Public Art Gallery
description:
A free public gallery on the Octagon with a mix of New Zealand and European art, from historic paintings to contemporary work, photography and sculpture. A rainbow light installation is a favourite photo spot.

There's a children's area, toilets and a café, so it's a good rainy day stop in the centre of town. It's open daily from 10am to 5pm.
Local tip: Start the street art trail from here, since the ROA tuatara on Bath Street is just off the Octagon.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm; free entry, donations welcome

name: Olveston Historic Home
description:
A 35-room Edwardian mansion built in 1904 for the businessman and collector David Theomin, and left as it was when his daughter died and gave it to the city. It opened to the public in 1966, full of original furniture, art from around the world and the family's vintage Fiat.

You can only see inside on a guided tour of about an hour, which costs $26.50 for adults and $15.50 for children aged 6 to 16, with several tours a day. The guides are consistently praised for their stories about the family and early Dunedin. The gardens are free to wander, and upstairs is by stairs only.
Local tip: Book ahead, since tours are small and fill up, and park on the street, since there's no on-site parking.
hoursNote: Guided tours only, several a day; booking recommended; upstairs not wheelchair accessible

name: Dunedin Street Art Trail
description:
More than 50 commissioned murals across central Dunedin, by local and international artists. Highlights include ROA's giant tuatara and Tyler Kennedy Stent's Ed Sheeran portrait on Bath Street, just off the Octagon, Pixel Pancho's steampunk jockey on Jetty Street, and DALeast's Haast eagle on Stafford Street.

It's free and self-guided, and you can walk it as a loop or pick out favourites, with plenty of cafés in the Warehouse Precinct along the way.
Local tip: Pick up the Dunedin Street Art Trail Guide from the i-SITE on the Octagon, or use the interactive map on the DunedinNZ website.
hoursNote: Outdoors, any time; best in daylight

name: Tunnel Beach Track
description:
A short, steep walk down through farmland to sandstone cliffs and arches on the coast south of the city, finishing at a hand-carved 1870s tunnel through the rock to a small hidden beach. It's 2km return and takes about an hour, easy but steep on the way back up.

The track reopened on 14 November 2025, after slips closed it for a year. The beach is tidal, with rogue waves, and isn't safe for swimming, and the cliffs can be slippery and unstable after rain. Dogs aren't allowed, and parking is limited.
Local tip: Check the tides and only go down to the beach around low tide, bring a torch for the caves, and don't leave valuables in the car.
hoursNote: No dogs; tidal beach, go near low tide; car park gate reported locked from about 5pm, check signs; limited parking

name: Sandfly Bay Track
description:
A walk down huge sand dunes to a wild beach on the Otago Peninsula, where sea lions often haul out on the sand. It's about 15 minutes across farmland to a viewing platform, and the rest of the way down is a steep sandhill, so the climb back is hard work. Allow about an hour.

Yellow-eyed penguins sometimes come ashore in the evening. Keep at least 20m from sea lions and 50m from penguins, never block a penguin's path to the sea, and stay on the marked track, since the dunes are eroding.
Local tip: Don't leave anything in the car, since there have been break-ins at the car park, and stay well back from sea lions, which can move surprisingly fast.
hoursNote: Open any time; steep sand climb back; keep 20m from sea lions, 50m from penguins; no drones near wildlife

name: Allans Beach
description:
A wild, white sand beach on the Otago Peninsula, reached by a 5 minute walk over farmland and through the dunes from the car park at the end of Allans Beach Road. It's one of the best places near Dunedin to see New Zealand sea lions, which haul out on the sand and sometimes sleep in the dunes, and fur seals are also common here.

From Hoopers Inlet, where sea lions raise their young, the road is gravel and needs care, so drive slowly, since sea lions sometimes cross it. There are no toilets at the beach, and the nearest are in Portobello. Swimming can be dangerous in strong wind and currents.
Local tip: Keep at least 20m from sea lions and seals and 50m from penguins, and look carefully as you walk through the dunes, since sea lions like to rest there.
hoursNote: Open any time; 5 min walk from the car park; gravel road past Hoopers Inlet; nearest toilets in Portobello; dogs on lead on the track

name: Pineapple Track
description:
A popular skyline walk from Booth Road in Glenleith, up through bush and open tussock towards Flagstaff, with views over the city, the harbour and the Taieri Plains. It takes about 2 hours return and is moderate, with most of it uphill on the way out.

It starts in forest with streams and tūī, then opens out with no shade near the top. It links to other tracks, but it isn't a loop, so most people come back the same way.
Local tip: Take a layer and water for the exposed upper section, and turn around at the top for the view back over Dunedin.
hoursNote: Open any time; exposed with no shade near the top; not a loop, return the same way

name: Ross Creek Reservoir
description:
A sheltered native bush reserve just above the city, around one of the oldest reservoirs in the country, built during the 1860s gold rush. The flat loop around the water takes 10 to 15 minutes, and short side tracks lead to School Creek Falls, a tall, narrow waterfall with a viewing deck.

There are several entrances and linked tracks, so you can make the walk as long as you like. It's a good choice on a windy day, when the hills and coast are too exposed.
Local tip: Use the Burma Road entrance for the easiest, pram-friendly route to the reservoir, and the Cannington Road entrance for the waterfall.
hoursNote: Open any time; flat reservoir loop, steeper to the waterfall; can be muddy

name: Royal Albatross Centre
description:
The only mainland breeding colony of royal albatross in the world, at Pukekura / Taiaroa Head on the tip of the Otago Peninsula. The one-hour Albatross Classic tour, from $71.55, includes a presentation, a short film and about 30 minutes in a glassed observatory watching the nesting birds.

The 90 minute Unique Taiaroa tour, from $82.07, adds the underground Fort Taiaroa, built in the 1880s, and combos add a harbour wildlife cruise or yellow-eyed penguin viewing. The drive out along the harbour takes about 45 minutes from the city, and seeing the birds in flight depends on the wind and the time of year.
Local tip: Book ahead in summer, since tours sell out, and stop for fish and chips in Portobello on the way back.
hoursNote: Listed daily from 10.15am; tours by booking; evening penguin tours at dusk

name: Orokonui Ecosanctuary
description:
A 307 hectare predator-fenced forest sanctuary about 20 minutes north of the city, where native birds such as kākā, takahē, kererū, bellbirds and South Island robins live wild and come close at the feeding stations. You can also see tuatara and skinks.

Self-guided entry is $27 for adults, $13 for children and $65 for a family, and the 1.5 hour guided tours are $65 for adults and worth it for spotting things you'd otherwise miss. There are tracks of different lengths through the forest, and the visitor centre has a café.
Local tip: It's closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and you need your own transport, so plan it as a morning on the way to or from the coast north of Dunedin.
hoursNote: Closed Tue and Wed; Thu to Mon 9.30am to 4.30pm; café 10am to 3pm

name: St Clair Beach
description:
The city's main beach, a long stretch of golden sand joining St Kilda, with a cluster of cafés and bars along the Esplanade at the St Clair end. It's a consistent surf break, and there are surfers in the water most days.

The water is cold all year, but the Esplanade is good for a walk and a coffee even when it's too cold to swim. Parking is free.
Local tip: Park at the St Clair end for the cafés and the hot salt water pool, or walk the whole beach to St Kilda and back for an easy, flat hour.
hoursNote: Open any time; cold water year round; free parking

name: St Clair Hot Salt Water Pool
description:
An outdoor seawater pool heated to 28 degrees, built into the rocks at the south end of St Clair beach, and the only survivor of several saltwater pools Dunedin built in the late 1800s. It has six lanes, and adults pay about $9 and children about $4.

There's a toddler pool, modern changing rooms and a café overlooking the surf. The pool is open only in the warmer months, roughly October to March.
Local tip: Swim laps while you watch the surfers on the point right next to the pool, then warm up in the café.
hoursNote: Seasonal, roughly October to March; 7.30am to 4pm; closed in winter

name: Signal Hill Lookout
description:
A hilltop lookout above the city with a 360 degree view over Dunedin, Otago Harbour, the peninsula and the ocean. It's about 10 minutes' drive from the centre, and there's a monument at the top.

The road up is narrow and parking is limited. It's very exposed, so it's often windy and cold even on a sunny day.
Local tip: Go at sunrise rather than sunset, since the hill looks east over the harbour, and take a warm jacket whatever the weather looks like below.
hoursNote: Open any time; narrow road, limited parking; very windy

name: Moeraki Boulders
description:
Te Kaihinaki, a beach about an hour north of Dunedin scattered with huge, almost perfectly round boulders, some up to 2m across and a few cracked open. They formed in mudstone laid down around 60 million years ago and were exposed as the cliffs eroded, and they're signposted on SH1, 3km south of Hampden.

There are two ways in. From the café at the end of a private road, a small fee gets you a track straight down to the beach and a 150m loop with a view from above, and the café does good seafood chowder. From DOC's free car park at Waiwherowhero Creek, it's a 10 minute walk along the beach, but there are no toilets there.
Local tip: Go at low tide, when more boulders are exposed, and at sunrise or sunset for the best photos. Watch for rogue waves on this exposed coast.
hoursNote: Beach open any time; best at low tide; café 8.30am to 4pm

name: Sutton Salt Lake
description:
New Zealand's only inland salt lake, in a dry basin of schist tors near Middlemarch. The lake has no outlet, so salts from the surrounding soils have built up over time. An easy 3.5km self-guided loop, 45 minutes to an hour, runs from the reserve entrance to the lake and back.

To get there, drive south from Middlemarch on SH87, and just after crossing the railway line for the second time, turn right onto unsealed Kidds Road. The entrance is about 2.5km along on the left. The lake is shallow and can dry out in summer, and the track isn't wheelchair accessible.
Local tip: There's no shade on the loop, so take a hat and water, and pair it with a day on the Otago Central Rail Trail from Middlemarch.
hoursNote: Open any time; 3.5km easy loop, 45 min to 1 hr; unsealed Kidds Road off SH87, about 9.5km from Middlemarch; not wheelchair accessible

name: Esplanade Surf School
description:
A surf school on the Esplanade at St Clair, running group and private lessons for beginners through to more advanced surfers, plus board and wetsuit hire. A 1.5 hour group lesson is $60 for adults and $45 for children aged 7 to 16, with the board and wetsuit included.

It's now under new management, and recent reviews praise the instructors. Lessons run through the warmer months and can be rescheduled if the surf or weather isn't right.
Local tip: Book ahead, by phone on 0800 484 141 or online, and confirm the day before, since lessons depend on the surf.
hoursNote: Operates roughly October to April; lessons by booking; prices on request

name: Warrington Domain Freedom Camping
description:
A free freedom camping area on a big grassed field by the beach at Warrington, about 25 minutes north of Dunedin. You can hear the waves from your van, there are portaloos and a dump station on site, and flush toilets and a sink are a minute's walk away by the playground.

Campers report that you don't need to be self-contained to stay here, but check the current signs. Stays are limited to two nights, and fires aren't allowed.
Local tip: The beach is a good surf and walking spot, and Orokonui Ecosanctuary is just up the road for the morning.
hoursNote: Free; max 2 nights; no fires; toilets and dump station; check signs for current rules

name: Hogwartz Backpackers
description:
An independent backpackers in a restored old home on Rattray Street, a short uphill walk from the Octagon. It has single beds rather than bunks, cosy rooms, a fire in the lounge, a piano and a big, well-stocked kitchen.

It's quieter than most hostels, and guests like the character of the building. Reception closes in the early evening, and hot water pressure can vary when the place is full.
Local tip: Arrive before reception closes, around 7pm, if you can, and don't be put off by the hill, since it's only a few minutes from town.
hoursNote: Reception closes early evening; check-in times on booking

name: George Street Motel Apartments
description:
A motel on upper George Street with spacious one-bedroom apartments that have full kitchens, big TVs and on-site parking. It's good value for a full apartment within walking distance of the centre and the museum.

Guests consistently mention how clean and warm the units are, and the friendly owners.
Local tip: It's an easy walk to the Otago Museum, the Botanic Garden and the George Street cafés, so you can leave the car parked.
hoursNote: On-site parking; rates vary by season

name: 97 Motel Moray
description:
A central motel on Moray Place, a couple of minutes' walk from the Octagon, with spacious studios and apartments with kitchenettes. The decor is a little dated, but the rooms are clean, comfortable and surprisingly quiet for the location.

The staff are helpful with local tips, and restaurants, bars and shops are all within walking distance.
Local tip: It's the easiest base for doing the city on foot, including the street art trail, which starts just around the corner off the Octagon.
hoursNote: Reception Mon to Fri 7am to 8pm, Sat and Sun 8am to 6pm
